info.bio: The Offspring es una de las bandas punk rock más exitosas de la historia con alrededor de 50 millones de discos vendidos. El grupo proviene de Orange County, California, originalmente formado en 1984. Actualmente está integrada por Dexter Holland, vocalista y guitarrista rítmico, Noodles, guitarrista, Greg K, bajista y Pete Parada, baterista. A pesar de que básicamente son una banda de punk y de rock alternativo incorporan muchos estilos como ska, grunge, hard rock y heavy metal entre otros.

scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.

mentions.text: …clubs for years: Face To Face, with Don't Turn Away (1992); Joykiller, formed by T.S.O.L.'s veterans; F.Y.P.; etc. Most successful of them all were Offspring (1), who competed with Green Day's mass appeal on Smash (1994). The Humpers sounded more sincere than the average of these clones of Screeching…

podcast.title: Name Change Inspiration (1986)
podcast.body: The band changed its name to The Offspring in 1986 after members watched a B-movie titled "The Offspring: They Were Born To Kill." "but that changed to the offspring in 1986. After everyone saw a B movie called The offspring, they were born to kill."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Single Warped Tour Show (1997)
podcast.body: The Offspring played only one show on the 1997 Warped Tour. "The offspring played one show."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Anarchy Airlines – Dexter Holland's Private Jet Fleet, Solo Round-the-World Flight 2004
podcast.body: *Smash* (1994) and subsequent Offspring albums generating more than 32 million in worldwide sales gave singer Dexter Holland the means to pursue his passion for aviation. He earned his first pilot's license in 1996, subsequently gaining more advanced certifications. He owns a Citation II twin-engine jet (approximately $2.5 million used), painted with the anarchy symbol on the tailfin and furnished with leopard-print interior — his own "Anarchy Airlines." He also flies an Aero Vodochody L-39 Czech/Russian jet fighter. He has enough simulator hours to pilot a 747. On November 25, 2004, Holland completed a secret solo circumnavigation: Los Angeles, New York, Iceland, Egypt, Dubai, Bangkok, Siberia, Russia, Alaska, and home — 11 days sustained almost entirely on beef jerky and Doritos, during which he encountered a volcanic eruption in Iceland, locusts in Egypt, and uncooperative customs officials in Russia. "Some people are into golf. Some people are into shooting deer. I'm into flying."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 2005 Renaissance
podcast.body: By spring 2005, The Offspring were "once hot again" and experiencing a "big-time renaissance" as rock music was on the ascendant. "The offspring and the Beastie boys were once hot again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Publishing Catalog Sale (2016)
podcast.body: In early 2016, The Offspring sold a portion of their publishing catalog for $50 million. This significant financial transaction helped their frontman, Dexter Holland, resolve outstanding payment issues with Cessna related to his private jets, which had led to a lawsuit and repossessions. "Then in early 2016 the offspring sold a chunk of their publishing catalog for $50 million which should clear up the plane problems."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: 924 Gilman Street Alumni
podcast.body: The Offspring are noted as alumni of 924 Gilman Street, the all-ages punk club in West Berkeley, California. Like other bands that signed with major labels, they are no longer welcome to perform at the club due to its strict "no major label bands" policy. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Accusations of Selling Out
podcast.body: As The Offspring achieved widespread popularity and transitioned to a major label, they, like other commercially successful pop punk bands, were accused of "selling out" by punk purists. "purists became annoyed, accusing groups like Green Dan, the offspring and Rancidov selling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Active Rock Radio Crossover
podcast.body: This band saw crossover airplay on active rock radio stations, helping the format become less of a niche. "But there was also some crossover with alternative rock stations, offspring, food fighters, bush and so on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Alaska Snowboarding Gig
podcast.body: Prior to their mainstream breakthrough, The Offspring secured a gig playing for snowboarders in Alaska, a trip that coincided with their song "Come Out and Play" beginning to explode on radio. "It got the band a sweet gig playing for a bunch of snowboarders up in Alaska. And it was while they were away that things got kind of crazy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Aviation Achievements and Financial Challenges
podcast.body: Dexter Holland is rated to fly executive jets, having obtained his pilot's license in 1996. In late 2004, he fulfilled a long-held ambition by flying solo around the world in a twin-engine Cessna Citation, covering 25,000 miles in 10 days while subsisting on Doritos and beef jerky. Although he once owned three planes, two were repossessed, and he faced a lawsuit over payment arrears for another. He resolved these debts by selling off some of The Offspring's publishing money, allowing him to fly freely again. "So in late 2004, he did it. He took a twin engine set-na citation, solo around the world. 25,000 miles and 10 days existing on, he says, Doritos and Beef jerky."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Biff Naked's Music Video Appearance
podcast.body: Biff Naked made an appearance in The Offspring's music video for their song "The Kids Aren't Alright." This cameo expanded her public visibility beyond her own musical projects. "if you know the offspring video the kids aren't all right she's in that one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: California Hardcore Scene
podcast.body: The Offspring were deeply rooted in the California hardcore scene, a fierce but small community dedicated to punk that evolved from the original 1970s punk. This music became a soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, including bands like Dead Kennedys, The Adolescents, The Vandals, Black Flag, and Bad Religion, which was niche and rarely played on radio. "Everyone was into California hardcore. The punk that evolved out of the original punk of the 1970s. The scene was small but fierce and its adherents stuck together. And some of this music became the soundtrack for skaters and snowboarders, dead candidates, the adolescence, the vandals, black flag, bad religion, really niche stuff at the time, and certainly stuff that never made it on the radio."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Career Choice over Academia
podcast.body: Despite being strongly encouraged by his professors to pursue a doctorate in molecular biology, Brian Holland decided to focus on his band, The Offspring, after realizing its potential success. This decision led to the band selling around 30 million records, making him significantly wealthier than a tenured professor. "he said, now you know this whole band thing is starting to work out. I think I'll try that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Certified Jet Pilot and Global Flight
podcast.body: Utilizing some of his earnings, Brian "Dexter" Holland became a certified jet pilot and owns a private jet. He notably completed a solo trip around the world in just 10 days, demonstrating his adventurous spirit and capabilities beyond music. "Oh, and did I mention that Dexter used some of his earnings to become a certified jet pilot?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Touring
podcast.body: The Offspring remained an active touring band into the 2010s, performing alongside other prominent pop punk acts. "So it was the offspring and Billy Towns and Fallout Boy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dexter Holland's Aviation Career and Plane Ownership
podcast.body: Dexter Holland is a certified jet pilot who has successfully flown solo around the world. He possesses a collection of three aircraft, which includes Cessna corporate jets and a retired Soviet-era fighter plane that he acquired from Estonia. He has accumulated sufficient flight hours in jets to be qualified to pilot a 747. "Dexter is a certified jet pilot who has flown solo around the world."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dexter Holland's Hot Sauce Business – Gringo Bendito
podcast.body: Dexter Holland, the singer for The Offspring, owns a hot sauce company called Gringo Bendito. The company manufactures its hot sauce in Newport Beach, California, producing approximately 120 gallons per week. It has expanded its distribution to grocery store chains and is served in several restaurants in Orange County. The brand's logo features Dexter dressed as a Mexican bandit. "If you've ever heard of Gringo Bendito, this is a brand of hot sauce. Dexter owns the company."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dexter Holland's Ibanez RG570 USA Custom
podcast.body: Dexter Holland of The Offspring frequently plays an Ibanez RG570 USA Custom guitar, possessing at least two versions with subtle variations in their finishes. In a music video for one of their songs, he is seen playing a version with a striking chrome top. "He's often seen playing in Ibanez RG570 USA Custom, he has at least two versions with slightly different finishes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 3

podcast.title: Dexter Holland's Software Development Interest
podcast.body: Dexter Holland has pursued an interest in software development, specifically working with software designed for the Blackberry. Although no product has been released yet, he has been in communication with Research in Motion regarding his efforts. "Dexter has been working with some software designed for the Blackberry."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dexter's Academic Prowess
podcast.body: Brian Holland, known by his nickname Dexter due to his exceptional performance in school, was the valedictorian of his high school graduating class. He later earned a bachelor's degree in biology and a master's degree in molecular biology from the University of Southern California, with his professors urging him to pursue a PhD. "His nickname is Dexter because he was so good in school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Discovered by Epitaph Records
podcast.body: The Offspring were a band that Epitaph Records "took a chance on," eventually leading to their significant success and establishing Epitaph as one of the most important indie labels globally. "They were the ones who took a chance on a band called The Offspring, and I think we all know how that story turned out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drummer Change and Early Demos
podcast.body: After their original drummer left to pursue a career as a gynecologist, the band began recording demos and selling cassettes, such as the collectible "six songs and tarantica sets," at their gigs. "After a drummer change, the original dude went off to learn how to be a gynecologist. Seriously, they began recording demos and tossing off cassettes that they'd sell at gigs. If you can find original copies of the six songs and tarantica sets, you've actually got something pretty collectible."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Releases
podcast.body: Before their first albums, the band released demos, at least one 7-inch single, and appeared on significant compilation records of the era. "There were demos, at least one seven inch single and a couple of spots on those oh so important compilation records of the day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fan of The Surf Punks
podcast.body: Members of The Offspring were fans of The Surf Punks, highlighting the significant influence The Surf Punks had on the punk and ska-punk bands emerging from Orange County in the 1990s. "Everybody in the offspring, for example, was a fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Focus on Fun Attitude
podcast.body: A defining characteristic of The Offspring's music, particularly exemplified by albums like Americana, was its emphasis on "having fun," despite retaining a punk edge. "Again, the music had a punk edge, but the attitude was, for the most part, about having fun."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Formation as Manic Subsidal
podcast.body: The band initially formed under the name Manic Subsital in the Huntington Beach area of Orange County, south of Los Angeles, comprising three high school students and the school's janitor. "They'd first come together as a group called Manic Subsital in the Huntington Beach area of Orange County, south of Los Angeles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hot Sauce Brand, Gringo Bandito
podcast.body: Dexter Holland is a connoisseur of hot sauces and has successfully launched his own line called Gringo Bandito, which is noted for its quality. "He has a line called, Gringo Bandito, which is actually pretty good."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: In-Depth History Coverage
podcast.body: The Offspring were among the specific performers profiled in-depth by the ongoing history program. "In-depth history is on bands like...The Off-Spring."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Influence of The Ramones
podcast.body: The Offspring is explicitly cited as one of the significant bands that would not have come into existence without the foundational impact and influence of The Ramones.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9

podcast.title: Involvement with Innocence Project
podcast.body: Brian "Dexter" Holland actively works with the Innocence Project, a non-profit legal clinic. This organization offers DNA testing to individuals convicted of crimes, helping them prove their innocence through scientific evidence. "Dexter works with a charity called Innocence Project, which is a non-profit legal clinic that offers DNA testing for people convicted of crimes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Jason McClain - Number One Fan
podcast.body: Jason McClain, a forklift operator and The Offspring's devoted number one fan, was recognized by the band with a small vocal part in their hit song "Come Out and Play," where he says the line "you gotta keep them separated." "Jason McClain. He was a forklift operator who was the offspring's number one fan. No matter where the band played, Jason was guaranteed to be in the audience. So as a reward, the band gave him a small part in that song. And that's Jason that says, you gotta keep them separated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Label Change to Columbia/Sony
podcast.body: The Offspring moved from their independent label, Epitaph, which had nurtured their early career, to Columbia Records, an imprint of the major label Sony. "by this time the offspring had jumped from Epitaph, the indie label that brought them up, to Columbia, an imprint of Sony, one of the major labels."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Late 90s Struggles
podcast.body: The Offspring, a band associated with the mid-90s punk revival, faced challenges around the close of the 1990s, which contributed to the broader sentiment that the punk revival had lost momentum and that the rock scene was in decline. "The punk revival of the middle 90s had run aground and bands like Green Day and the offspring were having struggles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 00's Part 1: The Sad State of Rock

podcast.title: Massive Sales on Epitaph
podcast.body: The Offspring achieved immense commercial success while signed to the independent label Epitaph. They were the "orange band" that eventually sold 20 million records on their own, a testament to Epitaph's ability to support and distribute successful artists without being a major label. "Until they signed this orange band called the offspring who eventually sold 20 million records on their own."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-1990s Punk Revival
podcast.body: The Offspring were mentioned as a band that contributed to the punk revival of the middle 1990s, a trend that followed in the wake of grunge's popularity. "It led to the punk revival of the middle 1990s, giving us Green Day in the offspring."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mid-90s Punk Rock "Holy Trinity"
podcast.body: The Offspring became one of three bands, alongside Green Day and Rancid, identified as the "holy trinity of punk rock" in the mid-1990s. "The offspring became part of the mid-90s holy trinity of punk rock, along with Green Day, who were also admirably filling the Kurt Cobain vacuum and Ransett, who sometimes sounded more clash than the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Noodles' Entry into the Band
podcast.body: Noodles, the guitarist, reportedly joined the band because he was the only member cool or old enough to purchase beer for the rest of the high school-aged group. "Apparently he got into the band because he was the only one cool enough or old enough to buy everyone else beer. That's how he got into the group."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Band Name
podcast.body: The group's original name was Manic Subsidal before changing to The Offspring. "The original name of the group was Manic Subcital."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: PhD in Microbiology and HIV Research
podcast.body: Dexter Holland holds a PhD in microbiology, which explains extended periods between The Offspring's albums. His 2017 thesis focused on HIV research and was titled "Discovery of mature microRNA sequences within the protein coding regions of global HIV-1 genomes, predictions of novel mechanisms for viral infection and pathogenicity." "So you want to know why the offspring went so long between albums? There you go. He was working as PhD."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Piracy and Discovery - Napster Era
podcast.body: During the era of digital file sharing platforms like Napster, Emule, and Kazaa, users could download entire discographies of bands like Offspring, not just single albums. This created a sensation of infinite abundance and allowed people to discover bands that weren't played on traditional radio. "ya no solo discos, sino discografías completas de extremo duro, de Nirvana o de Ophespring."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Por qué ya no elegimos nuestro tono de llamada?

podcast.title: Pop Punk Decline (2010s)
podcast.body: Despite the general decline of pop punk in the early 2010s, The Offspring, among other bands, persisted in the genre. "It never went away. I mean, we still had bands like Green Day and the offspring and Blink 2 and Panic at the disco."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 2: The Role of Indie Rock

podcast.title: Pop Punk Heritage Act
podcast.body: The Offspring was identified as one of the "Big Heritage Acts" of Pop Punk that kept the spirit of the genre alive in the 2010s, despite its popularity being nowhere near its 90s or 2000s peaks. There was also a sentiment in some punk circles to reclaim punk from "Corporatized Punk" exemplified by bands like The Offspring. "The Big Heritage Acts were still there, you know, offspring, link quantity to some 41 simple plan, and they kept the spirit alive." "There's also the sense in some quarters that Punk needs to be torn down and rebuilt, reclaimed from the so-called Croppered Punk, exemplified by Blink-Wentety 2-Some41 in the offspring."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of the 2010s Part 4: The Revivals

podcast.title: Pre-Smash Albums
podcast.body: Prior to the release of Smash, The Offspring had already put out two albums from Orange County, which were noted for performing "very well." "There's another group from Orange County that has given us two albums already, but they did very well."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Punk Revival Context
podcast.body: The Offspring were part of the punk revival movement in the 1990s. Their growing success helped pull other bands like Rancid into the mainstream, illustrating the ripple effect of popular punk revivalists on related scenes like third-wave Ska. "And as punk revivalists like Green Day and the offspring got bigger and bigger, Ranset was basically sucked up in their wake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Snowboarding Video Features
podcast.body: Some of The Offspring's songs began appearing in snowboarding videos, which helped set the stage for their wider recognition. "Plus some of these songs started showing up in snowboarding videos."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sonic Coincidence with The Beatles
podcast.body: The song "Why Don't You Get a Job?" released in 1998, is identified as a basic variation of The Beatles' "Ob-La-Di, Ob-La-Da," but it is characterized as an "unfortunate sonic coincidence" rather than plagiarism, given the extreme unlikelihood of deliberately plagiarizing the world's most famous rock band. "Is that plagiarism? Well, hardly. No one would be dumb enough to plagiarize the most famous rock band of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tours with Skate Punk Bands
podcast.body: The Offspring landed tours with Pennywise and other similar skate punk bands, establishing their presence in the scene. "They landed tours with Pennywise and a few other like-minded Skate Punk bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tremendously Successful Indie Punk Band
podcast.body: The Offspring, initially a "pure indie band" recording for Epitaph Records, demonstrated that an indie punk band could achieve tremendous success, selling 11 million copies of their third indie album and becoming a major force in the mid-90s punk rock revival. "Not only was this a punk band, but this was an indie punk band, and it was a tremendously successful indie punk band. Off-Spring, back when they were a pure indie band recording for Epitaph Records, they were a major, major part of the mid-90s punk rock revival."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unstoppable Sales
podcast.body: The Offspring were described as "unstoppable" in the early 2000s, selling albums by the tens of millions. "Meanwhile the offspring was unstoppable. Blink 182 was selling albums by the tens of millions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Final Show March 1, 1994; Death April 8, 1994 – The Vacuum That Reshaped 1994's Rock Landscape
xref.body: Nirvana played their final concert in Munich on March 1, 1994 — Kurt's voice was shot, the band was exhausted, and the rest of the European tour was canceled. On March 3, he deliberately overdosed on tranquilizers in a Rome hotel room. On March 18, police were called to his Seattle house after he locked himself in a room with guns. He agreed to enter rehab after an intervention, then escaped. His body was found April 8. The news was read on air: "Nirvana lead singer Kurt Cobain shot himself to death at a Seattle home yesterday." The effect on music fans was profound and prolonged. The loss of Nirvana's central narrative created a temporary opening that Green Day, The Offspring, Blur, and Oasis each rushed to fill. "Kurt's death was extremely traumatic. And the mourning continued for months."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Licensed Air Transport Pilot and Instructor (1996)
xref.body: Dexter Holland obtained his pilot's license in 1996 and is now a licensed air transport pilot and flight instructor. In November 2004, he completed a solo circumnavigation of the world in his twin-engine Cessna Citation, covering 25,000 miles in 10 days while subsisting solely on Doritos and beef jerky. He later faced financial issues with his aircraft, including a 2014 lawsuit from Cessna for nearly $1 million in arrears and the repossession of two planes, problems resolved by The Offspring's $50 million publishing catalog sale in 2016. "In November 2004 he flew his own twin-engine sesna citation around the world. 25,000 miles in 10 days, totally solo."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: By spring 2005, the Beastie Boys were "once hot again" and experiencing a "big-time renaissance" as rock music was on the ascendant. "The offspring and the Beastie boys were once hot again."

xref.title: 924 Gilman Street Alumni
xref.body: Green Day are alumni of the all-ages punk club 924 Gilman Street in West Berkeley, California. They were welcome there during their early "indie days," including when they recorded an original song in 1992. However, due to the club's strict rule against major label bands, Green Day is no longer permitted to play there, along with other successful punk acts. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

xref.body: Primus is identified as an alumnus of 924 Gilman Street, the influential all-ages punk club in West Berkeley, California. The club's rule prohibiting major label bands means that Primus, despite their roots there, is no longer welcome to perform. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

xref.title: 924 Gilman Street Alumni
xref.body: Bad Religion are counted among the alumni of 924 Gilman Street, the significant all-ages punk club in West Berkeley, California. Because of the club's stringent policy against major label bands, Bad Religion is no longer permitted to perform at the venue. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

xref.body: As their commercial success and mainstream visibility grew following their major label signing, Green Day faced criticism from punk purists who accused them of "selling out." "purists became annoyed, accusing groups like Green Dan, the offspring and Rancidov selling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Accusations of Selling Out
xref.body: As Rancid gained popularity and commercial recognition, they, alongside other successful pop punk bands like Green Day and The Offspring, were accused of "selling out" by punk purists. "purists became annoyed, accusing groups like Green Dan, the offspring and Rancidov selling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Blink-182's Manager
xref.body: Rick DeVoe became the manager for Blink-182, and he also managed other prominent bands such as The Offspring, No Effects, and Pennywise. He played a key role in raising Blink's profile, particularly within the snowboard community. "The band attracted a manager, a guy by the name of Rick DeVoe, who also worked with groups like The Offspring and No Effects in Pennywise."

xref.body: Died of a heroin overdose on May 25, 1996, after taking a "celebratory hit of heroin." This occurred just six weeks before Sublime's highly anticipated major label third album was scheduled to be released. "But before they could join the ranks of bands like Green Day and the offspring, the singer up and died of an overdose. His name was Bradley Noelle."

xref.title: Dual Revival Role
xref.body: Rancid descended from the hardcore punk band Operation Ivy, which had started incorporating Ska as early as 1987. Rancid figured prominently in both the punk revival and the third wave of Ska, benefiting from the growing popularity of punk revivalists like Green Day and The Offspring. "Then came Ranset, who figured in both the punk revival and third wave SCAT. And as punk revivalists like Green Day and the offspring got bigger and bigger, Ranset was basically sucked up in their wake."

xref.title: Epitaph Records Legacy
xref.body: After self-releasing their debut, Epitaph Records evolved into one of the most significant independent labels globally, famously taking a chance on The Offspring, which led to their success. "Now Epitaph, of course, would later become one of the most important indie labels in the entire world."

xref.body: Biff Naked maintained an active touring career, performing alongside internationally recognized acts such as the Foo Fighters, The Smashing Pumpkins, Green Day, and Snoop Dogg. She also appeared in The Offspring's "The Kids Aren't Alright" music video, showcasing broad industry engagement. "she had a great live run too performing with everyone from the food fighters and the smashing pumpkins to Green Day and Snoop Dogg and if you know the offspring video the kids aren't all right she's in that one."

xref.body: Sir Bob Geldof, of The Boomtown Rats and Live Aid fame, is the father of daughters Peaches Honey Blossom Michelle Charlotte Angel Vanessa, Fifi Trixibelle, and Pixie. "And if you want to read some really vicious stuff about the offspring of Sir Bob Geldoff, he of the Boomtown rats in Live Aid, look up stuff on his daughter, Peaches Honey Blossom, Michelle Charlotte Angel Vanessa."

xref.title: Financial Troubles and Publishing Catalog Sale
xref.body: Dexter Holland encountered significant financial difficulties related to his aircraft, including being sued by Cessna in 2014 for nearly $1 million in arrears on his jet payments, leading to the repossession of two other planes. His payment structure was eventually renegotiated to 71 monthly payments of around $10,000 each, plus a final payment of approximately $500,000. In early 2016, The Offspring sold a substantial portion of their publishing catalog for $50 million, which likely resolved his plane-related financial issues. "In 2014 he was sued by sesna for missing payments on his jet after falling nearly $1 million in a rears."

xref.title: Funding Epitaph Records
xref.body: The band Bad Religion funded Epitaph Records, a punk rock label based in Orange County, California. Like Merge Records, Epitaph was founded by a band seeking an alternative to the major label system, and it eventually achieved massive success with The Offspring. "Epitaph was funded by a band that was unsatisfied with the major label system. In this case, the group was Bad Religion."

xref.title: Influence on California Punk Revival
xref.body: The band had a significant impact on the California punk revival that emerged in the late 1980s, influencing many punk and ska-punk bands from Orange County in the 1990s, including The Offspring. "They were never really that popular outside of their home state, but like I said, they had a huge influence on the California punk revival that began in the late 1980s."

xref.title: Influence on Rock Music
xref.body: The Ramones are credited with profoundly influencing countless rock bands over several decades, with a direct lineage tracing back to their original version for bands like Rise Against, Metallica, Blink 182, Motorhead, Green Day, Guns N' Roses, The Clash, Sex Pistols, Rancid, The Pixies, The Beastie Boys, Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, The Strokes, The Offspring, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "virtually any rock band of the last 25 years, 35 years, and you can draw a line back into the past, and that line will inevitably lead back to the Ramones."

xref.body: Green Day, a prominent band from the mid-90s punk revival, experienced struggles around the end of the 1990s, contributing to the perception that the punk revival had run aground and that rock was in a difficult period. "The punk revival of the middle 90s had run aground and bands like Green Day and the offspring were having struggles."

xref.title: Mainstream Perception vs. Importance
xref.body: Although the mainstream treated The Ramones as a joke for decades, they were, in fact, one of the most important bands rock and roll had ever seen. Their foundational influence is noted as essential for bands like Green Day, Nirvana, The Offspring, and Pearl Jam.

xref.body: After releasing two independent albums, Sublime secured a major record deal with high expectations, believed to have the potential to achieve the same level of success as The Offspring or Green Day. xref.body: After acquiring astute management, Social Distortion stabilized, signed with a major label, and began producing alt-rock radio hits. Their management team was the same as The Offspring's, which allowed Social Distortion to benefit from The Offspring's surge in popularity. "But after finally acquiring some savvy management, social defund their footing, signed to a major label and started putting out alt-rock radio hits like this.
